catalog_metadata.purpose: Multi-site validation catalog for GLEWS detection pipeline (SBAS inversion -> velocity-change detection -> 51-pixel median spatial detrending -> z-score normalization -> DBSCAN clustering)

reference_validated_event.name: Gyirong / Bhotekoshi-Lhende Khola rock-ice avalanche (Nepal-Tibet border)
reference_validated_event.notes: Pipeline already validated against this event using NISAR L-band GUNW data.

catalog_metadata.key_finding_nisar_data_availability: ASF holdings show NISAR science-mode products (RIFG/RUNW/GOFF/GUNW/GCOV/GSLC) do not appear in volume until roughly mid-to-late July 2026 (earliest broad acquisitions ~2026-07-16/17), and dense repeat coverage at the specific sites checked below only begins ~2026-08-15 through 2026-08-22. This is materially later than the 'NISAR operational since 2025' assumption. Practical consequence: essentially NONE of the mid-2025 events (Blatten, Vallunaraju, Tracy Arm) have any pre-event or co-event NISAR imagery -- they are strictly ALOS-2 (or Sentinel-1 C-band cross-check) candidates, not NISAR validation candidates, despite occurring after NISAR's 2025 launch. Only the already-validated Nepal Aug 2026 event and the currently-unfolding Weisshorn (Randa) event have usable NISAR time series.

sites.name: Weisshorn East hanging glacier (above Randa), Valais, Switzerland
sites.status: ongoing / unresolved as of catalog date
sites.date_or_period: Under formal instability surveillance since late June 2026; repeated partial ice break-offs (>=3 in a single day) on 2026-08-24; situation still developing as of 2026-09-05
sites.event_type: hanging glacier instability / partial ice avalanches, potential future large collapse
sites.magnitude: Multiple partial break-offs; total collapse volume not yet determined (event unresolved)
sites.casualties: None reported; Randa raised its municipal alert level as a precaution

nisar_coverage.notes: Both ascending and descending geometry available -- good for resolving line-of-sight ambiguity on a steep north/east-facing slope. Coverage only spans ~3 weeks pre-catalog-date, so SBAS time series is currently short (2-3 epochs); more acquisitions needed to build a meaningful pre-failure velocity trend.

sites.suitability: high priority, but time-critical and data-limited
expected_challenges: Very short NISAR time series so far (~3 weeks of acquisitions) -- insufficient for robust SBAS velocity-change detection at present; needs to be re-run as new acquisitions accumulate
Steep ice/rock hanging glacier terrain -- high layover/foreshortening risk on a 45-50 degree slope viewed from a spaceborne SAR geometry; ascending+descending stacking recommended
Event is still unfolding -- 'success' cannot yet be scored against a known outcome, so this is a live forecasting test rather than a retrospective validation
Small hanging-glacier area may fall below the effective resolution/min-cluster-size the DBSCAN min_pixels setting expects; may need to loosen area threshold for this site
sites.success_definition: If NISAR data through end of Aug/early Sep 2026 shows a DBSCAN-flagged, statistically significant (z-score) velocity-change cluster co-located with the known unstable hanging glacier segment before any further major collapse, that is a real-time forecasting success. This is the one site where the pipeline could be run prospectively, not just retrospectively.

sites.name: Birch Glacier collapse / Blatten village burial, Lotschental, Valais, Switzerland
sites.date_or_period: 2025-05-28 (collapse); precursor rockfalls/creep acceleration from Bietschhorn onto glacier for weeks prior; village evacuated 2025-05-19
sites.event_type: rock-ice avalanche / glacier collapse burying a village
sites.magnitude: ~3,000,000 m3 of debris (glacier + rock); registered as a M3.1 seismic event
sites.casualties: 1 confirmed dead (shepherd outside evacuation zone), 1 missing; ~300 residents evacuated in time, no other deaths thanks to early evacuation

nisar_coverage.checked_via: asf_search platform=NISAR, POINT(7.8119 46.4142), start=2025-01-01 end=2025-06-15 -> 0 results; unrestricted date search -> earliest product 2026-08-22
nisar_coverage.notes: No NISAR acquisitions exist anywhere close to this event; NISAR's operational science-data record for this site only begins in Aug 2026, over a year after the collapse.

sites.suitability: excellent scientific case (extremely well-instrumented precursor with published pre-collapse velocity data from GNSS/terrestrial radar/optical feature tracking), but NOT usable for NISAR validation
sites.recommended_data_source: ALOS-2 L-band (PALSAR-2) StripMap, ascending/descending, 2024-2025 archive; Sentinel-1 C-band as a cross-check for the faster part of the acceleration (though C-band decorrelates quickly over active ice)
expected_challenges: No NISAR data -- must be run as an ALOS-2 validation instead, requiring separate acquisition/processing tooling
Very steep, high-relief alpine terrain with heavy layover from most viewing geometries

Glacier surface already fast-moving (0.8 to ~2 m/day pre-collapse) -- InSAR phase likely decorrelates in places the closer it gets to failure, which itself could be a detectable precursor signal (coherence-loss based, complementary to the velocity/z-score approach)
Published in-situ/ground-based data (ETH Zurich, GLAMOS, VAW) is dense enough for tight cross-validation against pipeline output
sites.success_definition: Would the pipeline's velocity-change detector flag the Bietschhorn/Birch Glacier area as anomalous in ALOS-2 imagery from spring 2025 (ideally weeks before the 2025-05-19 evacuation), independently reproducing what ground instruments already showed?

sites.name: Vallunaraju rockfall-triggered GLOF, Cordillera Blanca, Peru
sites.event_type: rockfall into proglacial lake -> glacier lake outburst flood (GLOF) / debris flow cascade
sites.magnitude: ~43,000 m3 released from lake drainage; small by rock-avalanche standards but high-consequence due to downstream city
sites.casualties: Multiple deaths reported; dozens of homes damaged/destroyed in Huaraz

nisar_coverage.checked_via: asf_search platform=NISAR, POINT(-77.4564 -9.4222), start=2025-01-01 end=2025-05-15 -> 0 results; unrestricted -> earliest product 2026-08-18

sites.suitability: marginal for this pipeline -- the triggering rockfall source area is small and rock (not glacier ice), and the primary hazard chain (lake drainage/debris flow) is hydrological rather than a slow-creeping mass the SBAS/velocity pipeline is built to catch
sites.recommended_data_source: ALOS-2 L-band if precursor creep on the rockfall source slope needs to be tested; otherwise better suited to optical/lake-area monitoring than InSAR velocity detection
expected_challenges: No NISAR data
Very small triggering rockfall volume -- likely below the pipeline's effective minimum detectable mass/area given the 51-pixel filter and DBSCAN min_pixels settings
High-relief tropical Andes terrain with rapid snow/ice melt noise
Event driven more by lake configuration change than by a long precursor creep signal -- may not have a multi-week velocity precursor to detect at all
sites.success_definition: Lower priority: mainly useful as a negative/edge case to characterize the pipeline's minimum detectable event size, not as a strong positive validation target.

sites.name: Tracy Arm fjord landslide / South Sawyer Glacier megatsunami, Alaska
sites.event_type: rock avalanche (not ice) into a fjord, preconditioned by glacier retreat; generated a 481 m runup megatsunami
sites.magnitude: ~64,000,000 m3 rock; seismic signal equivalent to M5.4
sites.casualties: None (occurred before cruise ships arrived for the day)

nisar_coverage.checked_via: asf_search platform=NISAR, POINT(-133.4022 57.9114), start=2025-01-01 end=2025-08-20 -> 0 results; unrestricted -> earliest product 2026-08-22

sites.suitability: borderline for THIS pipeline: this is a rock slope failure exposed by glacier retreat, not a glacier-ice collapse per se, but it is exactly the class of 'deglaciation-destabilized slope' GLEWS aims to flag, and it has an unusually good precursor record (days of escalating microseismicity before failure)
sites.recommended_data_source: ALOS-2 L-band ascending/descending over the Tracy Arm headwall; note Alaska has generally sparse ALOS-2 archive coverage compared to High Mountain Asia and the Alps, so archive availability should be checked before committing
expected_challenges: No NISAR data
Steep fjord-wall terrain with narrow SAR viewing geometries -- severe layover likely from many look directions
Remote/cloud-prone Southeast Alaska reduces optical cross-validation options
ALOS-2 archive density over this specific fjord is unconfirmed and may be thin
sites.success_definition: Would the pipeline detect accelerating rock-mass creep on the failed slope in the weeks before 2025-08-10, matching the documented pre-failure microseismicity escalation timeline?

sites.name: Gyirong / Bhotekoshi valley rock-ice avalanche (precursor to the validated 2026 event, same location)
sites.status: occurred, pre-NISAR (ALOS-2 candidate); same site as the already-validated 2026 event
sites.date_or_period: 2024-07 (reported precursor rock-ice avalanche in the same area)
sites.magnitude: Not yet quantified in sources reviewed
sites.casualties: Not reported as significant in sources reviewed

nisar_coverage.notes: Predates NISAR entirely; would require ALOS-2 or Sentinel-1.

sites.suitability: high scientific value: same site as the confirmed 2026 detection, so an ALOS-2 run here tests whether the site was ALREADY showing anomalous creep two years before the catastrophic 2026 collapse -- i.e., whether the hazard was flaggable far earlier than the NISAR record alone would suggest
expected_challenges: No NISAR data -- ALOS-2 only
Need to establish precise source-area geometry for the 2024 event, which is less well documented in English-language sources than the 2026 disaster
High Himalaya terrain, seasonal monsoon cloud cover irrelevant to SAR but relevant to any optical cross-check
sites.success_definition: If ALOS-2 time series 2023-2024 shows a velocity-change anomaly in the same cluster location later flagged by the validated NISAR run for 2026, this demonstrates multi-year lead time potential for the pipeline.

sites.name: Chamoli (Ronti Peak) rock-ice avalanche, Uttarakhand, India
sites.event_type: rock-ice avalanche -> long-runout debris flow -> flood cascade
sites.magnitude: ~26.9 x 10^6 m3 rock+ice detachment; travel distance >17.6 km, elevation drop 4300 m
sites.casualties: >200 killed or missing; two hydropower projects destroyed

nisar_coverage.notes: Predates NISAR by ~5 years; ALOS-2 (operating since 2014) is the correct sensor.

sites.suitability: excellent -- one of the most thoroughly studied rock-ice avalanches in the literature, including a published pre-collapse motion / precursor-detection study (Nature Hazards and Earth System Sciences) that used satellite geodesy to show measurable pre-failure displacement
expected_challenges: ALOS-2 archive coverage over this part of the Garhwal Himalaya needs to be confirmed for the 2019-2021 window
Existing published precursor-motion analysis provides a strong independent benchmark to validate pipeline output against -- this is close to a 'known-answer' test
High relief, seasonal snow cover complicate coherence in places
sites.success_definition: Pipeline should reproduce (or come close to) the pre-collapse displacement signal already published by Kumar et al. / ESA teams for the Ronti Peak source area using independent processing.

sites.name: Sedongpu Glacier recurring collapses / Yarlung Tsangpo river blockages, SE Tibet
sites.date_or_period: Recurring: Oct/Nov/Dec 2017, Jan/Jul 2018 (major detachment ~130x10^6 m3 blocking the Yarlung Tsangpo for ~60 hours), Mar 2021 (~50x10^6 m3)
sites.event_type: recurring glacier detachment / ice-rock avalanche causing river damming
sites.magnitude: Multiple events 50-130 x 10^6 m3; subsequent bed erosion of ~335x10^6 m3 measured 2018-2022
sites.casualties: >6000 residents relocated after 2018 event; river blockage threatened roads and hydropower

nisar_coverage.notes: All known major events predate NISAR; site already has a published early-warning radar system (NHESS 2023) that could be used as ground truth.

sites.suitability: excellent as a recurring/multi-event ALOS-2 time series case -- tests whether the pipeline can catch a SEQUENCE of collapses at one persistently unstable site, and there is already a dedicated early-warning-system paper against which to benchmark
expected_challenges: Extremely dynamic terrain with repeated large-scale morphology changes between events, complicating SBAS coherence across the full multi-year record
Remote SE Tibet; ALOS-2 archive density should be checked
Existing site-specific early warning system (NHESS 2023) provides a strong comparison baseline
sites.success_definition: Pipeline should flag anomalous velocity/creep in the lead-up to at least the well-documented Oct 2018 detachment and the Mar 2021 event using ALOS-2 archive data.

sites.name: Aru Range twin glacier collapses (Aru-1 and Aru-2), western Tibet
sites.event_type: gigantic glacier detachment (twin events, same glacier system)
sites.magnitude: ~68 x 10^6 m3 (Aru-1); debris ran out ~7 km into Aru Co lake, generating a ~20 m lake tsunami

nisar_coverage.notes: Predates NISAR by ~9 years; classic ALOS-2 case, and ALOS-2 was operating and has been used in the published mechanism studies already.

sites.suitability: excellent -- the original benchmark case in the glacier-detachment literature (Kaab et al. 2018, The Cryosphere) with a documented pre-collapse basal lubrication / englacial hydrology mechanism; twin collapses (2 months apart at the same site) give a natural repeat-test
expected_challenges: Remote, high-altitude, low-population western Tibet -- limited independent ground validation data compared to Chamoli/Sedongpu
Flat-topped, low-relief plateau glacier morphology is actually favorable for InSAR (less layover than steep alpine cases) but coherence over a two-month gap between Aru-1 and Aru-2 should be checked
ALOS-2 archive availability circa 2016 should be confirmed (early in ALOS-2 mission)
sites.success_definition: Pipeline should detect anomalous pre-collapse velocity at Aru-1 in spring/early-summer 2016, and ideally show the site remaining or becoming re-anomalous before the Aru-2 event two months later.
